source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 44% of people in Slovak Republic were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
21.1% of health spending in Slovak Republic was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
1.6% of people in Slovak Republic reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
15% of hospital care costs in Slovak Republic were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
3% of outpatient medical care costs in Slovak Republic were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
66% of dental care costs in Slovak Republic were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
31% of pharmaceutical costs in Slovak Republic were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
In contrast, government and compulsory insurance schemes paid over 90% of these costs in Czechia, the Slovak Republic, Sweden, Germany, Denmark and the United Kingdom.
In Mexico, the Slovak Republic and Poland, pharmaceuticals accounted for over 60% of OOP spending.
In some countries, doctors are paid predominantly by fee-for-service (as in Germany, Japan, Korea and the Slovak Republic).
Remote consultations cannot be distinguished and are included in a few countries (such as Austria from 2020, and Ireland, Japan, Latvia, the Netherlands, the Slovak Republic and Spain from 2019).
For example, in 2023, expenditure on medical goods represented around 30% of all health spending in the Slovak Republic and Greece.

In 2023, PHC represented 14% of all health spending on average across OECD countries, ranging from 10% or less in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and the Slovak Republic to around 20% in Lithuania, Estonia and Finland (Figure 7.16).

Overall, every third health dollar was spent on ambulatory providers in Belgium, Mexico, Finland, Luxembourg and the United States but this share was below 20% in Türkiye, Greece and the Slovak Republic.
